content: Why does docs#Ring extend docs#AddCommGroup and ocs#AddGroupWithOne instead of docs#AddCommGroupWithOne ? I suspect this changes nothing to your example above, but I did find it surprising.

Has anyone ever tried making the AddComm...WithOne classes the preferred parents over previous ...Ring classes? It would make the preferred parents tree much shallower, and therefore typeclass search faster overall. But it's hard to tell without trying it out

Yaël Dillies said:

Why does docs#Ring extend docs#AddCommGroup and docs#AddGroupWithOne instead of docs#AddCommGroupWithOne ? I suspect this changes nothing to your example above, but I did find it surprising.

Eric also asked that here https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/pull/38017#discussion_r3076202202 and I tried it in #39417 but the performance was poor.

Aaron asks whether extends Semiring, NonAssocRing, NonUnitalRing would be better. I interpret this as meaning "we don't really know what we're doing" (I certainly don't know what I'm doing). This is a question about how to design the algebra hierarchy and whether the "I make things 7 times as bad" Ring.toAddCommGroupWithOne is a bad thing or an inevitable thing.

I think the idea is to have two disjoint ancestors, one with all the data for the additive stuff (i.e., AddMonoid containing the addition and zero) and one with all the data for the multiplicative stuff (i.e., Monoid, containing multiplication and one). If you start extending `AddMonoidWithOne, you're breaking this disjunction.
5 messages were moved here from #mathlib4 > WithVal.instRing by Kevin Buzzard.

Sébastien Gouëzel said:

If you start extending `AddMonoidWithOne, you're breaking this disjunction.

Semiring extends MonoidWithZero which is a similar story I guess. I'll try redesigning Ring in the way Aaron suggests but we'll still need an instance to AddGroupWithOne I guess...
isn't AddGroupWithOne gettable through NonAssocRing?

Kevin Buzzard said:

Semiring extends MonoidWithZero which is a similar story I guess.

No. The direct inheritance line (with first parent) is Semiring -> NonUnitalSemiring -> NonUnitalNonAssocSemiring -> AddCommMonoid. So the AddCommMonoid is embedded faithfully in the semiring, no breaking / unbreaking involved. The zero from MonoidWithZero will be picked from this one.

But it's true that the Mul is not coming from an embedded Monoid, it's coming from the Distrib of NonUnitalNonAssocSemiring. If you think that the most important line is Semiring -> AddCommMonoid, then we have everything right. If If you think that's the multiplication, though, we are suboptimal. But I think one needs much more often to consider the underlying AddCommMonoid of a ring than its Monoid structure (who uses Monoids anyway? :-), so I guess anything breaking this direct line of inheritance will get worse performance.

If you want to see what exactly is broken to pieces and what is not with some definition, the thing to do is to #print Semiring, say, and look at the constructor. It looks like

constructor:
  Semiring.mk.{u} {α : Type u} [toNonUnitalSemiring : NonUnitalSemiring α] [toOne : One α]
    (one_mul : ∀ (a : α), 1 * a = a) (mul_one : ∀ (a : α), a * 1 = a) [toNatCast : NatCast α]
    (natCast_zero : ↑0 = 0 := by intros; rfl) (natCast_succ : ∀ (n : ℕ), ↑(n + 1) = ↑n + 1 := by intros; rfl)
    (npow : ℕ → α → α) (npow_zero : ∀ (x : α), npow 0 x = 1 := by intros; rfl)
    (npow_succ : ∀ (n : ℕ) (x : α), npow (n + 1) x = npow n x * x := by intros; rfl) : Semiring α

You see that the map to NonUnitalSemiring is a faithful embedding, same thing for toOne. The other ones (for instance to AddMonoidWithOne), mixing fields of the two structures, will necessarily involve some unfolding/refolding.

Kevin Buzzard said:

Aaron asks whether extends Semiring, NonAssocRing, NonUnitalRing would be better

Why not even just Semiring R, NonAssocRing R?

Mathematically it seems to check out:

import Mathlib

class Foo (R : Type*) extends Semiring R, NonAssocRing R where

instance (R : Type*) [Foo R] : Ring R where -- works

Is there a reason you also want to extend NonUnitalRing R @Aaron Liu ? Even extends Semiring R, NonUnitalNonAssocRing R is fine.

because otherwise we don't get this instance for free

import Mathlib

class Foo (R : Type*) extends Semiring R, NonAssocRing R where

-- fails
example {R : Type*} [Foo R] : NonUnitalRing R := inferInstance

I have tried the logic I'm advocating for above, i.e., separate cleanly the additive data and the multiplicative data, with direct parents for Semiring given by AddCommMonoid and Monoid, in #39467. That's a +6/-3 PR, with a 0.97% performance gain (-1.7T)!
Amazing! I suspected it would be a good change but I was afraid it would be counterbalanced by AddGroupWithOne not being preferred anymore
This is exactly the sort of story which makes me think that actually we need to sit down and think about how the algebra hierarchy is designed and how it should be designed. Thank you Sebastien!

I think a factor in the speedup is also that we short-circuit the seldom relevant classes NonUnitalNonAssocSemiring and so on, with now a direct path from Semiring to AddCommMonoid while before it had to go through 3 arrows. As it's something that happens all the time, that may help a lot.

Here is another example which came up in a conversation with Bhavik and Henrik Boving about why grind was being slow:

import Mathlib

set_option trace.profiler.useHeartbeats true in
set_option trace.profiler true in
set_option trace.Meta.synthInstance true in
variable (M : Type) [AddCommMonoid M] in
#synth AddSemigroup M -- [Elab.command] [172475.000000]

This is ludicrously slow, and the search goes all the way up to fields and then starts on normed stuff, Lie stuff, C^* algebras etc.
This one should be part of our main spine. We should probably bump a little bit the priority of arrows along this main spine, let me try to see if it makes a difference.
In contrast, the change to Ring at #39469 is a disaster.

I'm a little surprised this works, since I tried something similar in #7873 and it didn't work well. Maybe I did it wrong back then, or maybe something has changed significantly (we decoupled the algebraic and order hierarchies), or maybe it just didn't play well with the other changes in #7873. In any case, there are tricky interactions between extends order and instance priorities, so we should be careful.
By the way, the old benchmark results used to include a metric for typeclass inference. Is there still a way to benchmark that?

Also, I'm wondering if there's a way to benchmark the performance of typeclasses below Field in isolation. That way we wouldn't have to worry about the influence of other typeclasses extending the algebraic hierarchy, whose design may still need adjustment.

Sébastien Gouëzel said:

This one should be part of our main spine. We should probably bump a little bit the priority of arrows along this main spine, let me try to see if it makes a difference.

I've made the experiment in #39471. The outcome is not good (+0.22%). I think this should be a good change, but I claim that with current Lean any priority increase like that is doomed, for the following reason.

When we declare instances, by default they all have priority 1000. So, the fact that the product of AddMonoids is an AddMonoid has priority 1000, and so does the arrow from AddCommMonoid to AddMonoid, say. When trying to find an AddMonoid instance for α × β , both instances could be tried as they have the same priority. In this situation the system is clever: the more specific instances are tried first, so the product one is used directly, as it should. If we increase just a little bit the priority of AddCommMonoid.toAddMonoid, then its priority becomes strictly higher than the priority of the specific instance instAddMonoidProd, so we will go the wrong path. And that's bad because it can lead to explosion in situations where there is one obvious good instance.

Here is a mwe illustrating this:

def MyCopy (α : Type) : Type := α

class Foo (α : Type) where
instance (α : Type) : Foo (MyCopy α) where

class Bar (α : Type) extends Foo α where
instance (α : Type) : Bar (MyCopy α) where

variable {α : Type}

/- When synthetizing `Foo (MyCopy α)`, typeclass inference can just apply the
instance `instFooMyCopy`, or try to deduce it from `Bar.toFoo`. It tries the
more specific instance first, so makes the right choice. -/

/-- info: instFooMyCopy α -/
#guard_msgs in
#synth Foo (MyCopy α)

/- However, the two paths have exactly the same priority 1000, so increasing the
priority of `Bar.toFoo` breaks this and we take the wrong path.
-/

attribute [instance 1010] Bar.toFoo

/-- info: (instBarMyCopy α).toFoo -/
#guard_msgs in
#synth Foo (MyCopy α)

/- A solution is to increase the priority of the specific instances
like `instFooMyCopy` -/
attribute [instance 2000] instFooMyCopy

/-- info: instFooMyCopy α -/
#guard_msgs in
#synth Foo (MyCopy α)

There is a simple solution to this issue: when declaring an instance which is specific (i.e., it does not apply to a bare type, i.e., the indexing keys are not trivial), then use priority 2000 instead of 1000. Then we could increase by hand a little bit the priority of important instances, while keeping them lower than the priority of specific instances that should always be tried first. We could do the change from 1000 to 2000 for specific instances by hand throughout Mathlib, but I think that's a very bad idea: instead, it should be changed in the instance declaration algorithm. It's probably a one-line change in core.

Note that I expect that this change would have no performance impact for current Mathlib (not good, not bad) because specific instances are already tried before generic instances. So it's a little bit hard to argument that we need this change. But it would make further improvements possible, while they're impossible today.
TLDR: core, would you consider upgrading the priority of instances that don't always apply (i.e., with nontrivial indexing keys) from 1000 to 2000? @Sebastian Ullrich

Sébastien Gouëzel said:

Note that I expect that this change would have no performance impact for current Mathlib (not good, not bad) because specific instances are already tried before generic instances.

I'm not sure what you're claiming here and are you sure that it's true? I think that prio 1000 instances (which are surely >= 95% of all instances) are simply applied in the reverse order to the order in which they are defined. Even changing the order of imports in mathlib can affect typeclass inference! I think that there are speed-ups to be had here.

Sébastien Gouëzel is right. The order in which instances are applied is determined as follows:

  1. Higher (priority := ...) instances are tried first.
  2. More specific discrimination tree key instances are tried first (e.g. instAddMonoidProd is tried before AddCommMonoid.toAddMonoid).
  3. More recently declared instances are tried first (this can depend on import order).

As an aside, in simp this is similar, but subtly different:

  1. Higher simp ... lemmas are tried first.
  2. Less specific discrimination tree key simp lemmas are tried first.
  3. Older simp lemmas are tried first (this can depend on import order).

Oh this is news to me! What is the definition of "more specific discriminant tree key instances"? Does instSMulOfMul [Mul X] : SMul X X count as a "more specific discriminant tree key instance" than e.g. Algebra.toSMul [Algebra A B] : SMul A B or are they equally specific?

"X is more specific than Y" means "in the first place where they differ, X has something concrete where Y has a variable".

In particular, it does not care about variable repetitions, so SMul X X and SMul A B are equally specific. This is why your PR #38704 gave such a big speedup :)

Kevin Buzzard said:

I'm not sure what you're claiming here and are you sure that it's true? I think that prio 1000 instances (which are surely >= 95% of all instances) are simply applied in the reverse order to the order in which they are defined.

My example above is designed precisely to show this: the instance Bar.toFoo is defined after instFooMyCopy, but still it's instFooMyCopy which is tried first because it is more specific.
Thanks a lot to both of you! I had been unaware of this subtlety and its exact nature until now.

Following up on @Sébastien Gouëzel's PR that changes the definition of Semring to not extend things like NonUnitalNonAssocSemiring, I have made #39719, which adds shortcut instances so that we avoid synthesizing instances that go through rarely used classes like NonUnitalNonAssocSemiring. This came up when @Kevin Buzzard and I were looking at some unification traces, and I saw some NonUnitalNonAssocSemiring floating around, which I thought would be best to avoid.

The result is another -0.52% speedup of mathlib.

It turns out that I had missed a crucial shortcut instance in my above PR. I've now added it in #40153, and this gives an additional 0.78% speedup of mathlib.

class Semiring (α : Type u) extends AddCommMonoid α, MonoidWithZero α, NonUnitalSemiring α,
  NonAssocSemiring α

I discovered this phenomenon independently a few weeks ago (when I was experimenting with changing the definition of Ring); the reason I discovered it was that a linter complained that I had made a definition without a docstring, but I knew that instances did not need docstrings. I am surprised that a linter did not complain that Semiring.toAddCommMonoid needed a docstring here.

Now that we have all of these shortcut instances leading the search to Semiring, it would be a good idea to thing about the relative priorities of general Semiring instances.

In #40156, I made an attempt at this, lowering the priority of DivisionSemiring.toSemiring. I tried this because it is tried as one of the first instances, but for unification purposes it looks like a suboptimal instance. The outcome is curious: an overal speedup of 0.24%, but the biggest changes are all slowdowns.
